extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of political science or American political history
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and evaluating the characteristics, foundations, and vitality of political parties (particularly U.S. parties) — their principles, tendencies, organization, and behavior on issues across historical periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles as the soul of a party
rubrics_metrics.description: What life is to an organism, principles are to a party; when the principles which are its soul have vanished, its body ought to dissolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party without guiding principles loses moral life and should, theoretically, dissolve; in practice parties may persist but are then fetid or pestiferous. Loss of principles leads to degeneration into mere factions or contests for office alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent opposition — centralized (national) vs federated (state) government
rubrics_metrics.description: One permanent opposition running through party history is between a centralized or unitary and a federated government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a party by which side of this fundamental question it represents: autonomy of communities (traditionally Democratic) versus majesty/beneficent activity of the national government (Federalists, Whigs, Republicans).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent opposition — liberty vs order
rubrics_metrics.description: The opposition between valuing the freedom of the individual as the first social good and valuing the checking and regulation of individual impulses (love of liberty vs love of order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess where a party falls on the spectrum: those distrusting human nature favor authority and restraint (Hamiltonian/Federalist tendency); those optimistic about human nature favor leaving individuals free (Jeffersonian tendency). The wisest balance avoids tyranny or anarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party organization and the patronage/spoils principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The development of complex machinery of party organization rests largely on the principle that public office is to be enjoyed only by the adherents of the President for the time being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the extent and centrality of patronage in party structure — strong patronage systems indicate organized party machinery and can shape party behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control by a dominant faction or interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may pass under the control of a particular interest or faction (e.g., by 1852 the Democratic party had passed almost completely under the control of the slave-holders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how much a party's doctrine and actions are determined by dominant internal factions or external interests; such control can produce doctrinal changes (e.g., constitutional dogmas) and direct party policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability and capacity for transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: A new era calls for the evolution of new parties or the transformation of the old ones by the adoption of tenets suited to the needs of the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a party can evolve its principles and programmes to address new problems; failure to adapt indicates lack of vital force and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditions and tendencies versus clear-cut principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither of the great parties often has anything definite to say as a party on many issues; both have traditions and tendencies but lack clean-cut principles or distinctive tenets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between a party's historical tendencies/traditions and explicit, actionable doctrines; heavy reliance on vague tradition instead of clear principles reduces predictability and seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational inertia and persistence despite loss of principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may hold together long after their moral life is extinct because members have formed habits of joint action, hatreds, prejudices, and leaders have advantage in using these habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the role of organizational habits, networks, and leadership interests in keeping a party functioning even when it lacks substantive principles — explains persistence of parties in absence of coherent doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness to electoral demographics and constituency interests
rubrics_metrics.description: On issues like temperance, parties' stances are shaped by the makeup of their voting blocs (e.g., Irish voters, German voters, Southern whites), so practical consequence is what they can gain or lose electorally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess party positions by examining constituency pressures and demographic alliances; parties often moderate or avoid positions that would alienate key groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and commitment on policy issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties frequently are unpledged or divided on concrete issues (e.g., regulation of liquor, tariff policy), leaving them without decisive answers to many policy questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a party's vitality by whether it takes clear, committed stances on pressing policy issues; vacillation or internal division indicates weakness or opportunism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical use and expansion of federal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may act as defenders or expanders of federal authority in practice (e.g., Republicans during the Civil War defended the Union and stretched Federal power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate parties by their actual record in using central power when circumstances demand; theoretical tendencies may be subordinated to practical calculations and majorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual and moral life (tradition that ennobles party action)
rubrics_metrics.description: English parties retained intellectual and moral life in principles which made their behavior predictable and ennobled struggles for office by connecting them to great objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence of an intellectual/moral core or tradition that gives members a sense of higher purpose; this sustains principled action even when leaders are unworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propensity toward corruption and patronage-seeking
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties are susceptible to corruption, frauds, and influence by wealthy interests (e.g., accusations that Republicans were corrupt and the 'party of the rich').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate frequency and severity of corrupt practices, lobbying, and patronage-seeking; such tendencies shape public perception and can replace principle with pursuit of office and favors.
